topics.name: Montgomery, Alabama
topics.kicker: Capital of Alabama · First Confederate capital and civil rights landmark
topics.briefing: Montgomery, on the Alabama River, has been Alabama’s capital since 1846. In 1861, the Confederacy was founded there, and Jefferson Davis took his oath as its president at the state capitol, so the city is nicknamed the “Cradle of the Confederacy.” Less than a century later, Rosa Parks’s arrest there sparked a 381-day bus boycott led by Martin Luther King Jr., and in 1965 voting-rights marchers from Selma ended their 54-mile walk at that same capitol.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This city was formed in 1819 when two towns on the Alabama River merged, and it was named for an Irish-born general who died leading an American attack on Quebec in 1775. In 1846, it replaced Tuscaloosa [“tusk-uh-LOO-suh”] as its state’s capital.
tossups.r: In 1861, it became the first capital of the Confederacy. For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama.

tossups.p: Jefferson Davis lived in this city in a house now known as the First White House of the Confederacy. On February 18, 1861, he took the oath of office as the Confederacy’s provisional president on the portico of its state capitol.
tossups.r: This city is nicknamed the “Cradle of the Confederacy.” For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama.

tossups.p: In April 1861, Confederate Secretary of War LeRoy Pope Walker telegraphed orders from this city telling P. G. T. Beauregard [“BOH-ruh-gard”] to demand the surrender of Fort Sumter. Delegates from seceded Southern states had met here two months earlier to form a new nation.
tossups.r: Jefferson Davis took his oath of office here. For 10 points, name this Alabama city, the first Confederate capital before Richmond.

tossups.p: On December 5, 1955, thousands of people packed into and around Holt Street Baptist Church in this city to hear a 26-year-old minister speak about a protest that had begun that morning. That minister, the pastor of this city’s Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, was chosen to lead the protest.
tossups.r: It was a bus boycott sparked by the arrest of Rosa Parks. For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama.

tossups.p: In May 1961, a mob attacked Freedom Riders, including John Lewis, when their bus arrived at this city’s Greyhound station, which now houses a museum about the rides. The next night, federal marshals protected a crowd meeting at Ralph Abernathy’s First Baptist Church here.
tossups.r: In 1955, Rosa Parks was arrested on a bus in this city. For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama.

tossups.p: Water flows across a round black granite table carved with the names of 41 people who died during the civil rights movement at a memorial in this city designed by Maya Lin. That memorial stands outside the offices of the Southern Poverty Law Center.
tossups.r: Martin Luther King Jr. led a bus boycott here in 1955 and 1956. For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama.

tossups.p: Hundreds of steel monuments, one for each U.S. county where racial terror lynchings were documented, fill the National Memorial for Peace and Justice, which opened in this city in 2018. Lawyer Bryan Stevenson’s Equal Justice Initiative also opened the Legacy Museum here.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Alabama city where Rosa Parks’s arrest started a famous bus boycott.

tossups.p: In his January 1963 inaugural address at the state capitol in this city, Governor George Wallace vowed to defend segregation. That capitol stands at the top of Dexter Avenue, a block from the church where Martin Luther King Jr. had been pastor.
tossups.r: In 1965, voting-rights marchers from Selma ended their 54-mile walk at that capitol. For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama.

tossups.p: On March 25, 1965, Martin Luther King Jr. asked “How long?” and answered “Not long” in a speech in front of this city’s capitol, saying that “the arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice.”
tossups.r: His listeners had just finished a march from Selma. For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama.

tossups.p: F. Scott Fitzgerald met his future wife, Zelda Sayre, the daughter of a judge, at a dance in this city while he was stationed at a nearby army camp in 1918. A house the couple rented here in the early 1930s is now a museum about them.
tossups.r: Zelda had been born here in 1900. For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama, where Rosa Parks was arrested in 1955.

tossups.p: The country singer Hank Williams is buried in this city, which has a museum devoted to his music, and the singer and pianist Nat King Cole was born here in 1919. The Alabama River flows past its downtown.
tossups.r: Martin Luther King Jr. was a pastor here when he led a bus boycott in 1955. For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama.

tossups.p: In 1910, the Wright brothers opened a civilian flying school in this city, on land that later became Maxwell Air Force Base. That base is home to the Air University, which trains Air Force officers.
tossups.r: This city on the Alabama River was the Confederacy’s first capital. For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama.

tossups.p: L. B. Sullivan, a city commissioner in charge of this city’s police, sued _The New York Times_ for libel over a 1960 advertisement supporting Martin Luther King Jr. The Supreme Court ruled against him in 1964, making it harder for public officials to win libel suits.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Alabama city where King had led a bus boycott in 1955 and 1956.

tossups.p: Jo Ann Robinson, an English professor at this city’s Alabama State College, used the school’s copying machine to print thousands of leaflets calling for a one-day protest. Her group, the Women’s Political Council, had complained to city leaders about segregated buses for years.
tossups.r: That protest grew into a 381-day bus boycott. For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama.

tossups.p: In March 1955, fifteen-year-old Claudette Colvin was arrested for refusing to give up her bus seat in this city. She later joined _Browder v. Gayle_, a lawsuit against bus segregation named partly for this city’s mayor, W. A. Gayle.
tossups.r: Nine months after Colvin’s arrest, Rosa Parks was arrested here too. For 10 points, name this capital of Alabama.

trap.title: Montgomery, Selma, or Birmingham?
trap.body: Three Alabama cities are famous civil rights answers. The 1965 voting-rights march began in Selma, where state troopers attacked marchers on “Bloody Sunday” at the Edmund Pettus Bridge, and it ended in Montgomery. Birmingham is where King wrote his “Letter from Birmingham Jail” in 1963 and where a bombing at the 16th Street Baptist Church killed four girls. Some questions also want the Montgomery Bus Boycott itself, not the city.
trap.fix: Montgomery clues: the state capital, the Confederacy’s first capital, Jefferson Davis’s oath, Rosa Parks, Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, and the end of the march. Selma clues: the Edmund Pettus Bridge and Bloody Sunday. Birmingham clues: Bull Connor, the Children’s Crusade, and the 16th Street Baptist Church. If the question says “this event” or “this protest,” answer “Montgomery Bus Boycott.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Montgomery, Alabama (do not accept “Alabama” or “Selma”)

topics.name: NAACP
topics.kicker: Civil rights organization founded in 1909 · Fought segregation in court
topics.briefing: The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People was founded in 1909, on the 100th anniversary of Abraham Lincoln’s birth, by Black and white reformers including W. E. B. Du Bois, Ida B. Wells, and Mary White Ovington. Du Bois edited its magazine, _The Crisis_, and its lawyers, led by Thurgood Marshall, won _Brown v. Board of Education_ in 1954. Rosa Parks was secretary of its Montgomery branch, and Medgar Evers led its work in Mississippi.
topics.answerHtml: NAACP (or National Association for the Advancement of Colored People)
accept: national association for the advancement of colored people
national association for advancement of colored people

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: After a deadly race riot in Springfield, Illinois, in 1908, William English Walling wrote an article called “The Race War in the North,” asking who would come to the aid of Black Americans. Mary White Ovington answered by meeting with Walling to plan this group.
tossups.r: It was founded the next year. For 10 points, name this civil rights organization that published _The Crisis_.

tossups.p: Oswald Garrison Villard, a grandson of the abolitionist William Lloyd Garrison, wrote “the Call” that led to the founding of this group in New York. Villard owned the _New York Evening Post_ newspaper.
tossups.r: The Call came out on Lincoln’s 100th birthday, in 1909. For 10 points, name this civil rights organization whose lawyers later won _Brown v. Board of Education_.

tossups.p: In 1921, this group’s monthly magazine, then edited for literature by Jessie Redmon Fauset [“FAW-set”], published Langston Hughes’s poem “The Negro Speaks of Rivers,” which Hughes had written as a teenager while riding a train to Mexico.
tossups.r: W. E. B. Du Bois edited that magazine, _The Crisis_, for more than twenty years. For 10 points, name this civil rights group founded in 1909.

tossups.p: The biologist Ernest Everett Just received the first of this group’s top awards in 1915, a medal named for its leader Joel Spingarn. Later winners of that Spingarn Medal include Jackie Robinson and Martin Luther King Jr.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this civil rights group, founded in 1909, whose lawyer Thurgood Marshall argued _Brown v. Board of Education_.

tossups.p: This group’s first president, the Boston lawyer Moorfield Storey, had once been Senator Charles Sumner’s secretary. In 1917, Storey won _Buchanan v. Warley_, in which the Supreme Court struck down a Louisville law that kept Black and white families on separate blocks.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this civil rights organization that W. E. B. Du Bois helped found in 1909.

tossups.p: In July 1917, this group led thousands of people in a Silent Parade down New York’s Fifth Avenue to protest racial violence, including a deadly riot in East St. Louis. James Weldon Johnson, who helped organize that march, became this group’s first Black executive secretary in 1920.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this organization whose magazine, _The Crisis_, was edited by W. E. B. Du Bois.

tossups.p: In the 1920s and 1930s, this group flew a flag reading “A Man Was Lynched Yesterday” outside its New York office. Walter White, who later led the group, secretly investigated dozens of lynchings in the South.
tossups.r: It also pushed the Dyer anti-lynching bill, which passed the House in 1922. For 10 points, name this civil rights organization founded in 1909.

tossups.p: Charles Hamilton Houston planned this group’s legal campaign against segregated schools, starting with lawsuits against all-white law and graduate schools in the 1930s. In 1940, his former student founded this group’s Legal Defense Fund.
tossups.r: That student, Thurgood Marshall, later won _Brown v. Board of Education_. For 10 points, name this civil rights group.

tossups.p: In _Smith v. Allwright_, this group’s lawyers persuaded the Supreme Court in 1944 to strike down the all-white primary elections that Texas Democrats used to keep Black citizens from voting.
tossups.r: Thurgood Marshall argued that case. For 10 points, name this civil rights organization whose Legal Defense Fund later won _Brown v. Board of Education_.

tossups.p: This group’s first field secretary in Mississippi investigated the 1955 murder of Emmett Till and organized boycotts before he was assassinated outside his home in Jackson in 1963. His widow, Myrlie Evers-Williams, chaired this group’s national board from 1995 to 1998.
tossups.r: That field secretary was Medgar Evers. For 10 points, name this civil rights organization founded in 1909.

tossups.p: In 1956, Alabama banned this group from operating in the state and demanded its list of members, but in 1958 the Supreme Court ruled that the group did not have to hand over the names.
tossups.r: Rosa Parks had been secretary of its Montgomery branch. For 10 points, name this civil rights group.

tossups.p: Daisy Bates, who led this group’s branches in Arkansas, advised the nine Black students who integrated Little Rock Central High School in 1957. In the 1940s, Ella Baker had traveled across the South as this group’s director of branches.
tossups.r: Its magazine was _The Crisis_. For 10 points, name this civil rights organization founded in 1909.

tossups.p: In 1915, this group organized protests against D. W. Griffith’s film _The Birth of a Nation_, which glorified the Ku Klux Klan. That same year, it filed a brief in _Guinn v. United States_, in which the Supreme Court struck down Oklahoma’s “grandfather clause” for voting.
tossups.r: W. E. B. Du Bois was one of its founders. For 10 points, name this civil rights group founded six years earlier.

tossups.p: At the 1963 March on Washington, this group’s leader, Roy Wilkins, announced that one of its founders had died in Ghana the night before. That founder had edited this group’s magazine for more than twenty years.
tossups.r: That founder was W. E. B. Du Bois. For 10 points, name this civil rights organization founded in 1909.

tossups.p: The journalist Ida B. Wells, who exposed lynching in her pamphlet _Southern Horrors_, and the educator Mary Church Terrell were among the signers of the call to found this group. Each year, this group honors performers of color with its Image Awards.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this civil rights organization whose lawyers won _Brown v. Board of Education_.

Its lawyers, led by Thurgood Marshall, won _Brown v. Board of Education_ (1954)
Rosa Parks was secretary of its Montgomery, Alabama, branch
Founders included Ida B. Wells, Mary Church Terrell, Mary White Ovington, Oswald Garrison Villard, and William English Walling

_The Crisis_ first published Langston Hughes’s “The Negro Speaks of Rivers” (1921); Jessie Redmon Fauset was its literary editor
_Smith v. Allwright_ (1944): Thurgood Marshall won the case that ended Texas’s all-white primary elections
Alabama banned it in 1956 and demanded its membership lists; the Supreme Court sided with the group in 1958

trap.title: Which civil rights group?
trap.body: Several civil rights organizations show up as answers. The NAACP (1909) fought mostly through lawsuits and lobbying. The Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC, 1957) was Martin Luther King Jr.’s group of Black ministers, the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC, 1960) grew out of the sit-ins, and the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE, 1942) organized the 1961 Freedom Rides. The Niagara Movement (1905) came just before the NAACP, and many of its members joined it.
trap.fix: NAACP clues: 1909, Lincoln’s 100th birthday, W. E. B. Du Bois and _The Crisis_, the Spingarn Medal, Thurgood Marshall and _Brown v. Board_, Medgar Evers, and Rosa Parks as a branch secretary. Saying “NAACP” is enough; you don’t need the full name.
trap.line: Real answer line: NAACP (or National Association for the Advancement of Colored People)

topics.name: NAFTA
topics.kicker: Trade pact of the U.S., Canada, and Mexico · In force 1994–2020
topics.briefing: NAFTA, the North American Free Trade Agreement, removed most tariffs, or taxes on imports, on goods traded among the United States, Canada, and Mexico. Leaders of the three countries signed it in 1992, Congress approved it in 1993, and it was in force from January 1, 1994, until a new deal called the USMCA replaced it in 2020. Supporters said it would boost trade, while critics such as Ross Perot warned that jobs would move to Mexico.
topics.answerHtml: NAFTA (or North American Free Trade Agreement; prompt on free trade agreement; do not accept “USMCA”)
accept: the north american free trade agreement
reject: canada united states free trade agreement
general agreement on tariffs and trade
free trade area of the americas

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: On the day this agreement took effect, rebels calling themselves the Zapatista [“zah-pah-TEE-stah”] Army of National Liberation launched an uprising in the Mexican state of Chiapas [“chee-AH-pahs”]. Their spokesman, Subcomandante Marcos, opposed the agreement.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this trade deal among the United States, Canada, and Mexico that began on January 1, 1994.

tossups.p: In November 1993, Vice President Al Gore defended this agreement in a televised debate on CNN’s _Larry King Live_ against a Texas billionaire who opposed it, about a week before the House voted on it.
tossups.r: That opponent, Ross Perot, had warned of a “giant sucking sound” of jobs going to Mexico. For 10 points, name this trade deal with Canada and Mexico.

tossups.p: U.S. Trade Representative Carla Hills led the American side in negotiating this agreement, which was signed in December 1992 by George H. W. Bush, Brian Mulroney of Canada, and Carlos Salinas [“sah-LEE-nahs”] of Mexico.
tossups.r: Congress approved it the next year. For 10 points, name this trade pact that took effect in 1994.

tossups.p: This agreement replaced a 1988 free-trade deal between the United States and Canada, which had been the main issue in that year’s Canadian election, won by Brian Mulroney’s Progressive Conservatives.
tossups.r: Mexico joined the talks for this wider deal. For 10 points, name this trade agreement that took effect on January 1, 1994.

tossups.p: To win votes in Congress, Bill Clinton’s trade representative, Mickey Kantor, negotiated two side agreements to this deal in 1993, one on workers’ rights and one on the environment. The environmental side deal created the Commission for Environmental Cooperation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this trade agreement that the United States, Canada, and Mexico launched in 1994.

tossups.p: In November 1993, the House approved this agreement by a vote of 234 to 200, with more Republicans than Democrats voting yes, even though House Majority Leader Dick Gephardt, a Democrat, opposed it.
tossups.r: The Senate passed it three days later. For 10 points, name this trade deal with Canada and Mexico.

tossups.p: Chapter 11 of this agreement set up a system called investor-state dispute settlement, which let companies from one member country take another member’s government to international arbitration over unfair treatment of their investments.
tossups.r: It phased out most tariffs among its three members. For 10 points, name this 1994 trade agreement among the U.S., Canada, and Mexico.

tossups.p: Less than a year after this agreement took effect, a sudden crash in the value of the Mexican peso led the Clinton administration to arrange billions of dollars in emergency loans for Mexico in 1995.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this trade pact among the United States, Canada, and Mexico, which Ross Perot had opposed.

tossups.p: Factories called maquiladoras [“mah-kee-lah-DOR-ahs”] that assemble goods in northern Mexico for export expanded quickly after this agreement took effect. The last tariffs it phased out, including Mexico’s tariffs on American corn and beans, ended in 2008.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this trade agreement signed by leaders of the U.S., Canada, and Mexico in 1992.

tossups.p: In 2018, at a summit in Buenos Aires, Donald Trump, Justin Trudeau, and Enrique Peña Nieto [“PAYN-yah nee-AY-toh”] signed a deal to replace this agreement; Canadians call the new deal CUSMA, and Mexicans call it T-MEC.
tossups.r: That replacement, the USMCA, took effect on July 1, 2020. For 10 points, name this 1994 trade pact among the United States, Canada, and Mexico.

tossups.p: Congress voted on this agreement under “fast track” rules, which allowed only a yes-or-no vote with no amendments, and the Senate approved it by a vote of 61 to 38 in November 1993.
tossups.r: It took effect at the start of the next year. For 10 points, name this trade deal among the United States, Canada, and Mexico.

tossups.p: Mexican president Carlos Salinas de Gortari [“sah-LEE-nahs day gor-TAR-ee”], who had studied at Harvard, pushed for this agreement in the early 1990s as part of his plan to open Mexico’s economy to foreign trade and investment.
tossups.r: He signed it in 1992 with George H. W. Bush and Brian Mulroney. For 10 points, name this trade pact that took effect in 1994.

tossups.p: In September 1993, former presidents Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter, and George H. W. Bush joined Bill Clinton at the White House to support this agreement as he signed its side deals on labor and the environment.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this trade pact among the United States, Canada, and Mexico that took effect on January 1, 1994.

tossups.p: Opponents of this agreement included the AFL-CIO and other labor unions, many environmental groups, and political figures as different as Pat Buchanan and Ralph Nader, while many business groups supported it.
tossups.r: Ross Perot warned it would cause a “giant sucking sound.” For 10 points, name this trade deal among the U.S., Canada, and Mexico.

tossups.p: Although this agreement was negotiated by a Republican administration, the Democratic president who followed made passing it a top goal, even though many labor unions and many members of his own party opposed it.
tossups.r: That president, Bill Clinton, signed it into law in December 1993. For 10 points, name this trade pact among the United States, Canada, and Mexico.

trap.title: NAFTA or the USMCA?
trap.body: The USMCA (United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement) replaced NAFTA on July 1, 2020, and questions about one can sound like the other. Clues about Donald Trump, Justin Trudeau, the 2018 signing, CUSMA, or T-MEC point to the newer deal, unless the question asks for the deal it replaced. Other trade answers include GATT and the World Trade Organization (worldwide), CAFTA (with Central America and the Dominican Republic), and the Trans-Pacific Partnership, and NATO is a military alliance, not a trade deal.
trap.fix: NAFTA clues: signed in 1992 by Bush, Mulroney, and Salinas; passed under Clinton in 1993; began January 1, 1994; Ross Perot’s “giant sucking sound”; and the Zapatista uprising. Listen for dates: 1992 to 1994 means NAFTA, and 2018 to 2020 means the USMCA.
trap.line: Real answer line: NAFTA (or North American Free Trade Agreement; prompt on free trade agreement; do not accept “USMCA”)

topics.name: Nathan Hale
topics.kicker: Patriot spy executed by the British in 1776 · Connecticut’s state hero
topics.briefing: Nathan Hale was a 21-year-old Yale graduate and Connecticut schoolteacher when he volunteered to spy on the British on Long Island in September 1776. Disguised as a schoolmaster, he was caught and executed by the British on September 22, 1776. According to later accounts, his last words were “I only regret that I have but one life to lose for my country,” and Connecticut later made him its official state hero.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This man’s most famous words may have been inspired by a line in Joseph Addison’s play _Cato_ about dying “but once to serve our country.” A British officer, John Montresor, later told American officers about this man’s calm last moments.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this patriot spy who supposedly said, “I only regret that I have but one life to lose for my country.”

tossups.p: This man was captured on September 21, 1776, the same day a great fire swept through British-occupied New York City. He was taken to the headquarters of General William Howe.
tossups.r: Howe ordered him executed the next day without a trial. For 10 points, name this Connecticut schoolteacher who had been spying for George Washington.

tossups.p: This officer belonged to Knowlton’s Rangers, an elite scouting unit whose commander was killed at the Battle of Harlem Heights while this officer was behind enemy lines on Long Island.
tossups.r: He had volunteered when George Washington asked for a spy. For 10 points, name this Connecticut patriot executed in 1776.

tossups.p: Posing as a schoolmaster looking for work, this man crossed Long Island Sound from Norwalk, Connecticut, to gather information about British troops. He carried his college diploma as part of his disguise.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American spy who was captured and executed by the British in September 1776.

tossups.p: This man’s Yale classmate and friend Benjamin Tallmadge later organized the Culper Ring, a spy network based in New York City and on Long Island that gave George Washington much better information about the British than this man had been able to gather.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this patriot spy who supposedly regretted having “but one life to lose” for his country.

tossups.p: After graduating from Yale in 1773, this man taught school in East Haddam and then at the Union School in New London, Connecticut, before joining the army in 1775. Both of those schoolhouses are now museums.
tossups.r: In 1776, he volunteered to spy on the British. For 10 points, name this Connecticut patriot who was executed that September.

tossups.p: A copy of Bela Pratt’s statue of this man, whose original stands outside Connecticut Hall at Yale, was placed at the headquarters of the Central Intelligence Agency in Langley, Virginia.
tossups.r: Connecticut later named him its official state hero. For 10 points, name this patriot spy executed by the British in 1776.

tossups.p: Frederick MacMonnies’s 1890s bronze statue of this man stands in City Hall Park in lower Manhattan, the island where he died in 1776, only three years after graduating from Yale.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this patriot spy who supposedly said, “I only regret that I have but one life to lose for my country.”

tossups.p: This man’s grandnephew, a Boston minister, wrote the 1863 story “The Man Without a Country,” about an army officer sentenced to spend the rest of his life on Navy ships without ever hearing news of the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Connecticut schoolteacher who was executed as a spy in 1776.

tossups.p: This man’s friend William Hull, who later surrendered Detroit to the British in the War of 1812, reportedly tried to talk him out of his dangerous mission and later recorded his famous last words.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Connecticut patriot who was executed after spying on the British in 1776.

tossups.p: This man was born in 1755 in Coventry, Connecticut, where his family’s homestead is now a museum, and he was only 21 years old when he died. His older brother Enoch went to Yale with him.
tossups.r: He was a captain in the Continental Army when he volunteered to spy behind British lines. For 10 points, name this patriot executed in September 1776.

tossups.p: After George Washington’s army lost the Battle of Long Island in August 1776, this young captain volunteered to slip behind enemy lines and find out where the British would strike next.
tossups.r: He was caught and executed that September. For 10 points, name this patriot spy who is the official state hero of Connecticut.

tossups.p: According to one account, the Loyalist ranger Robert Rogers tricked this man into revealing his mission by pretending to be a fellow patriot. Rogers had become famous leading a unit of rangers in the French and Indian War.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this American spy executed by the British in 1776, who supposedly regretted having “but one life to lose” for his country.

tossups.p: As a Yale student, this man joined the Linonian [“lih-NOH-nee-un”] Society, a club for debate and literature, and he graduated in 1773 at age 18, only three years before his death.
tossups.r: He later taught school and then spied for George Washington. For 10 points, name this Connecticut patriot executed in 1776.

tossups.p: While this man was behind enemy lines in September 1776, the British landed at Kips Bay and captured New York City. He was caught as he tried to make his way back to the American lines.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Connecticut schoolteacher and spy who supposedly said, “I only regret that I have but one life to lose for my country.”

trap.title: Hale or André?
trap.body: Two famous spies were executed during the Revolution. Nathan Hale was an American captain caught on a mission for George Washington in 1776. John André was a British major caught in 1780 while helping Benedict Arnold plot to hand over West Point, and the Americans executed him. Players also mix up Hale’s “one life to lose” with Patrick Henry’s “Give me liberty, or give me death!”
trap.fix: Hale clues: Yale, Connecticut schoolteacher, Long Island, Knowlton’s Rangers, 1776, and “one life to lose.” André clues: Benedict Arnold, West Point, captured near Tarrytown, and papers hidden in his stocking. Patrick Henry was a Virginia speaker, not a spy. Saying just “Hale” is enough.

topics.name: Oregon Trail
topics.kicker: 2,000-mile wagon route to the Pacific Northwest · Busiest 1840s–1860s
topics.briefing: In the 1840s and 1850s, tens of thousands of pioneers packed covered wagons in towns like Independence, Missouri, and set out on a 2,000-mile trip to Oregon’s Willamette Valley. Pulled mostly by oxen, the wagons followed the Platte River, crossed the Rockies at South Pass, and passed landmarks like Chimney Rock and Independence Rock. The journey took four to six months, and many travelers died of diseases like cholera.
topics.answerHtml: Oregon Trail (prompt on Oregon or Oregon-California Trail; do not accept “Santa Fe Trail,” “California Trail,” or “Lewis and Clark”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1906, Ezra Meeker, who had traveled this route as a young man in 1852, retraced it with an ox-drawn covered wagon to campaign for marking it before it disappeared.
tossups.r: This route began in towns like Independence, Missouri. For 10 points, name this roughly 2,000-mile trail to the Pacific Northwest.

tossups.p: Francis Parkman’s 1849 book named for this route describes his 1846 summer on the Great Plains, including weeks spent with a band of Lakota Sioux [“luh-KOH-tuh SOO”] near a fort in present-day Wyoming.
tossups.r: That fort, Fort Laramie, was a major stop on this route. For 10 points, name this wagon trail from Missouri to Oregon.

tossups.p: In 1971, three student teachers in Minnesota created a computer game named for this route, in which players buy oxen, ford rivers, and often lose members of their party to dysentery. The Minnesota Educational Computing Consortium later sent the game to schools across the country.
tossups.r: Real pioneers on it usually traveled in covered wagons pulled by oxen. For 10 points, name this wagon route that ran from Independence, Missouri, to Oregon.

tossups.p: Jesse Applegate wrote “A Day with the Cow Column” about the 1843 “Great Migration,” when about a thousand pioneers and their herds of cattle traveled this route together, helped along by the missionary Marcus Whitman.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this trail that took pioneers from Missouri to Oregon’s Willamette [“wih-LAM-it”] Valley.

tossups.p: In 1836, Narcissa Whitman and Eliza Spalding became the first white women known to cross the Continental Divide, traveling much of this route with their missionary husbands. The Whitmans were killed at their mission near Walla Walla in 1847.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this trail from Independence, Missouri, to Oregon that pioneers followed in covered wagons.

tossups.p: Travelers on this route hoped to reach a huge granite landmark in Wyoming by the Fourth of July, and so many carved their names into it that it was called the “Register of the Desert.”
tossups.r: That landmark is Independence Rock. For 10 points, name this trail that led wagon trains from Missouri to Oregon.

tossups.p: Wagons on this route crossed the Continental Divide at a broad, gentle gap in Wyoming that fur trader Robert Stuart used in 1812 and mountain man Jedediah Smith’s party crossed again in 1824.
tossups.r: That gap is South Pass. For 10 points, name this trail that ran from Missouri to the Willamette [“wih-LAM-it”] Valley.

tossups.p: Before Sam Barlow opened a toll road around the south side of Mount Hood in 1846, travelers on this route had to float their wagons on rafts down the dangerous Columbia River from The Dalles [“DALZ”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this trail whose travelers ended their trip in Oregon’s Willamette [“wih-LAM-it”] Valley.

tossups.p: Chimney Rock, a tall spire in western Nebraska, was the landmark that travelers on this route mentioned most often in their diaries. To get there, they followed the shallow Platte River, said to be “a mile wide and an inch deep.”
tossups.r: The trip usually took four to six months. For 10 points, name this roughly 2,000-mile trail that pioneers took to Oregon.

tossups.p: Near Fort Hall, a trading post founded by Nathaniel Wyeth [“WY-eth”] in 1834 in present-day Idaho, many travelers left this route and headed southwest toward California. Those who stayed on it followed the Snake River west.
tossups.r: Most travelers had started out from Missouri. For 10 points, name this pioneer trail that ended in Oregon’s Willamette [“wih-LAM-it”] Valley.

tossups.p: John McLoughlin, the Hudson’s Bay Company’s chief at Fort Vancouver, helped many tired and hungry American settlers who arrived at the end of this route, earning the nickname “Father of Oregon.” He worked for a British company, but he gave the newcomers food, seeds, and supplies on credit.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this trail that pioneers took from Independence, Missouri, to the Pacific Northwest.

tossups.p: In the 1851 Treaty of Fort Laramie, the United States promised yearly payments to Plains nations such as the Lakota and Cheyenne in return for safe passage for travelers on this route.
tossups.r: Most of those travelers walked beside their wagons. For 10 points, name this wagon trail that ran from Missouri to Oregon.

tossups.p: Wagon wheels on this route wore ruts several feet deep into soft sandstone near Guernsey [“GURN-zee”], Wyoming. Travelers on it burned dried buffalo dung, called “buffalo chips,” as fuel on the treeless plains.
tossups.r: Most of them walked beside wagons pulled by oxen. For 10 points, name this roughly 2,000-mile pioneer trail to Oregon.

tossups.p: Pioneers on this route said they were going to “see the elephant,” a phrase for facing great hardship, and the most common cause of death among them was the disease cholera. Drownings at river crossings were another common danger.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this trail that began in Independence, Missouri, and ended in Oregon.

tossups.p: Peter Burnett, who later became the first governor of the state of California, helped lead a large wagon train along this route in 1843. Travel on this route fell off after the first transcontinental railroad was finished in 1869.
tossups.r: Many of its travelers began in Independence, Missouri. For 10 points, name this pioneer trail to Oregon’s Willamette [“wih-LAM-it”] Valley.

trap.title: Which trail west?
trap.body: Several westward routes are separate answer lines. The Santa Fe Trail, opened in 1821, was a trade route from Missouri to Santa Fe, New Mexico. The California Trail shared the Oregon Trail’s eastern half, including Chimney Rock, Independence Rock, and South Pass, then split off toward the Sierra Nevada, and the Donner Party was on it. The Mormon Trail ran from Nauvoo, Illinois, to the Great Salt Lake, and the Lewis and Clark Expedition (1804–1806) traveled mostly by river, decades before the wagon trains.
trap.fix: Oregon Trail clues: the Willamette Valley, Oregon City, The Dalles, the Barlow Road, the Columbia River, the Whitmans, Fort Vancouver, and the 1843 Great Migration. Santa Fe clues: William Becknell, trade goods, and Bent’s Fort. California clues: the Humboldt River, the Sierra Nevada, Sutter’s Fort, and the Donner Party. Brigham Young means the Mormon Trail.

topics.name: Patrick Henry
topics.kicker: Virginia orator of the Revolution · “Give me liberty, or give me death!”
topics.briefing: Patrick Henry failed as a storekeeper and a farmer before he found his true talent: speaking. As a young Virginia lawyer and lawmaker, he blasted the Stamp Act in 1765, and in 1775 he urged Virginians to arm themselves with the cry “Give me liberty, or give me death!” He became the first governor of the independent state of Virginia, then fought the new U.S. Constitution as a leading Anti-Federalist.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the 1763 Parson’s Cause, this young lawyer argued that a king who struck down a useful Virginia law had “degenerated into a tyrant,” and the jury awarded the minister James Maury only one penny in damages.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Virginian who later declared, “Give me liberty, or give me death!”

tossups.p: Soon after joining the House of Burgesses in 1765, this man introduced resolutions against the Stamp Act and warned that “Caesar had his Brutus, Charles the First his Cromwell.” When other members shouted “Treason!” he supposedly answered, “If this be treason, make the most of it.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Virginia orator who later cried, “Give me liberty, or give me death!”

tossups.p: At the First Continental Congress in 1774, this delegate declared that “the distinctions between Virginians, Pennsylvanians, New Yorkers, and New Englanders are no more. I am not a Virginian, but an American.” John Adams recorded those words in his notes.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Virginian who in 1775 declared, “Give me liberty, or give me death!”

tossups.p: No written copy of this man’s most famous speech survives; the version known today was pieced together by William Wirt for an 1817 biography, more than forty years later. In that speech, he warned that “the next gale that sweeps from the north will bring to our ears the clash of resounding arms.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Virginian who ended that 1775 speech with “Give me liberty, or give me death!”

tossups.p: This speaker said he had “but one lamp by which my feet are guided, and that is the lamp of experience,” and later asked, “Is life so dear, or peace so sweet, as to be purchased at the price of chains and slavery?”
tossups.r: He gave that speech at St. John’s Church in Richmond in March 1775. For 10 points, name this patriot who ended it, “Give me liberty, or give me death!”

tossups.p: After Virginia’s royal governor, Lord Dunmore, had gunpowder removed from the public magazine in Williamsburg in April 1775, this man led a militia company toward the capital and won payment for the powder.
tossups.r: A month earlier, he had declared, “Give me liberty, or give me death!” For 10 points, name this Virginia patriot.

tossups.p: As governor, this man sent George Rogers Clark on a 1778 expedition to capture British posts in the Illinois Country, where Clark’s men took Kaskaskia and later Vincennes. This man served three straight one-year terms in that office.
tossups.r: In 1776, he had become the first governor of the independent state of Virginia. For 10 points, name this patriot who said, “Give me liberty, or give me death!”

tossups.p: At Virginia’s 1788 ratifying convention, this man asked what right the framers had to say “We, the people” instead of “We, the states.” He had refused to attend the Constitutional Convention, reportedly saying that he “smelt a rat.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Virginia Anti-Federalist who once cried, “Give me liberty, or give me death!”

tossups.p: This man spoke against the Constitution for days at Virginia’s 1788 ratifying convention, but James Madison’s side won by a vote of 89 to 79. He then helped keep Madison out of the first U.S. Senate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Anti-Federalist who demanded a bill of rights and once cried, “Give me liberty, or give me death!”

tossups.p: In a 1773 letter to a Quaker, this man admitted that he enslaved people although he believed slavery was wrong, writing, “I will not, I cannot justify it.” Ten years earlier, he had become famous as a lawyer in the Parson’s Cause.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Virginian who said, “Give me liberty, or give me death!”

tossups.p: In 1795, this former Anti-Federalist turned down George Washington’s offer to make him secretary of state. Four years later, Washington persuaded him to run for Virginia’s legislature, and he won but died before he could take his seat.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this patriot who said, “Give me liberty, or give me death!”

tossups.p: This man spent his last years at Red Hill, his plantation in Charlotte County, Virginia, where he died in 1799. He had been born in Hanover County, where he first won fame as a lawyer.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Virginia patriot who declared, “Give me liberty, or give me death!”

tossups.p: In 1941, the first Liberty ship, a type of cargo vessel mass-produced during World War II, was launched in Baltimore and named for this man. Two Virginia counties had also been named for him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Virginia orator who in 1775 declared, “Give me liberty, or give me death!”

tossups.p: As a young man, this future orator failed as a storekeeper and as a farmer before he taught himself enough law to become an attorney. His first famous case was the Parson’s Cause, argued at the Hanover County courthouse.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Virginian who said, “Give me liberty, or give me death!”

tossups.p: As a law student, Thomas Jefferson listened from a doorway of the House of Burgesses as this man spoke against the Stamp Act in 1765. This man had joined that assembly only days earlier, as a member from Louisa County.
tossups.r: Jefferson later succeeded him as governor of Virginia. For 10 points, name this orator who in 1775 declared, “Give me liberty, or give me death!”

trap.title: Which Revolutionary speaker?
trap.body: Several patriots are known for one famous line. Patrick Henry said “Give me liberty, or give me death!” in Virginia in 1775. Nathan Hale, a Connecticut spy, supposedly said “I only regret that I have but one life to lose for my country,” and James Otis of Massachusetts is linked to the slogan “Taxation without representation is tyranny.” Fellow Virginians Richard Henry Lee, who proposed independence in June 1776, and Henry “Light-Horse Harry” Lee also have “Henry” in their names.
trap.fix: Henry clues: the Parson’s Cause, the Stamp Act resolutions, “If this be treason,” St. John’s Church, first governor of Virginia, and leading the Anti-Federalists. Richard Henry Lee clues: the June 1776 resolution for independence. Saying just “Henry” is enough, but never say “Lee.”

topics.name: Paul Ryan
topics.kicker: Speaker of the House, 2015–2019 · Mitt Romney’s 2012 running mate
topics.briefing: Paul Ryan grew up in Janesville, Wisconsin, and was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives in 1998, when he was only 28. As chairman of the House Budget Committee, he became known for writing his party’s budget plans. He ran for vice president with Mitt Romney in 2012, served as Speaker of the House from 2015 to 2019, and chose not to run for reelection in 2018.

tossups.p: This congressman’s budget plans, including a 2011 plan called “The Path to Prosperity,” proposed large cuts in federal spending and major changes to Medicare. Those plans passed the House but not the Senate.

trap.title: Which Speaker is it?
trap.body: Twenty-first-century Speakers of the House get mixed up. John Boehner of Ohio was Speaker from 2011 until he resigned in 2015, Paul Ryan of Wisconsin served from 2015 to 2019, and Nancy Pelosi of California, the first woman Speaker, held the job from 2007 to 2011 and again from 2019 to 2023. Kevin McCarthy, Ryan’s fellow _Young Guns_ author, became Speaker in 2023. Other famous Ryans, like the baseball pitcher Nolan Ryan, are different answers.
trap.fix: Ryan clues: Janesville, the House Budget Committee, “The Path to Prosperity,” Mitt Romney’s 2012 running mate, the debate with Joe Biden, and the 2017 tax law. Boehner clues: Ohio and resigning in 2015. Pelosi clues: California and being the first woman Speaker. Saying just “Ryan” is enough.
trap.line: Real answer line: Paul Ryan (accept Paul Davis Ryan)

topics.name: Potomac River
topics.kicker: River of the nation’s capital · Divides Maryland from Virginia
topics.briefing: The Potomac River flows from the mountains of West Virginia to the Chesapeake Bay, forming much of the border between Maryland and Virginia. George Washington was born near it, made his home at Mount Vernon on its banks, and picked a spot along it for the nation’s capital. On the way, it meets the Shenandoah River at Harpers Ferry and tumbles over the rocky Great Falls just upstream from Washington, D.C.
topics.answerHtml: Potomac River (do not accept “Chesapeake Bay” or “Shenandoah River”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Maryland’s border with Virginia runs along the low-water mark on this river’s southern bank, so Maryland owns almost the entire width of the river where it separates the two states.
tossups.r: George Washington’s home, Mount Vernon, overlooks this river from the Virginia side. For 10 points, name this river that flows past Washington, D.C.

tossups.p: On July 4, 1828, John Quincy Adams turned the first shovelful of dirt for a canal that eventually ran 184 miles beside this river, from Georgetown to Cumberland, Maryland. Justice William O. Douglas later led a hike along that canal’s towpath to save it from becoming a highway.
tossups.r: George Washington’s Mount Vernon overlooks it. For 10 points, name this river that flows past Washington, D.C., into the Chesapeake Bay.

tossups.p: George Washington was the first president of the Patowmack Company, which built short canals to carry boats around the rapids of this river. In 1785, delegates from Virginia and Maryland met at George Washington’s home to settle arguments over shipping and fishing on it.
tossups.r: That meeting helped lead to the Constitutional Convention. For 10 points, name this river along which the national capital was built.

tossups.p: Thomas Jefferson wrote that the view where this river meets the Shenandoah [“shen-un-DOH-uh”] was “worth a voyage across the Atlantic.” The town at that meeting point, Harpers Ferry, was the site of John Brown’s 1859 raid on a federal armory.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this river that forms much of the border between Maryland and Virginia.

tossups.p: This river’s North Branch begins at the Fairfax Stone in West Virginia, a marker that once showed the edge of Lord Fairfax’s huge land grant. Farther downstream, this river flows past Cumberland, Maryland, and Harpers Ferry.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this river that flows past Washington, D.C., on its way to the Chesapeake Bay.

tossups.p: Below its Great Falls, this river rushes through Mather Gorge, named for the first director of the National Park Service. Georgetown grew up as a port just downstream, where the river’s falls stopped ships sailing up from the ocean.
tossups.r: It empties into the Chesapeake Bay. For 10 points, name this river that divides Washington, D.C., from Virginia.

tossups.p: George Washington, James Monroe, and Robert E. Lee were all born in Westmoreland County, Virginia, on the Northern Neck, a peninsula between this river and the Rappahannock [“rap-uh-HAN-uk”]. Lee was born at Stratford Hall there.
tossups.r: Washington later lived at Mount Vernon, on this river’s banks. For 10 points, name this river that flows past the nation’s capital.

tossups.p: Robert E. Lee’s army crossed this river to invade Maryland in September 1862 and retreated back across it at Boteler’s Ford after the Battle of Antietam [“an-TEE-tum”]. The Union’s main army in the East was named for this river.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this river that flows past Washington, D.C., into the Chesapeake Bay.

tossups.p: After hiding for days in a Maryland pine thicket, John Wilkes Booth and David Herold crossed this river by rowboat into Virginia in April 1865. Its lower stretch forms the border between southern Maryland and Virginia’s Northern Neck.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this river that flows past Washington, D.C., and George Washington’s Mount Vernon.

tossups.p: John Quincy Adams liked to swim in this river early in the morning while he was president. An island in it near Georgetown is a memorial to Theodore Roosevelt.
tossups.r: The Kennedy Center and the Lincoln Memorial stand near its banks. For 10 points, name this river that flows past Washington, D.C.

tossups.p: In 1608, Captain John Smith sailed up this river while exploring the Chesapeake Bay region, meeting the Patawomeck and other Algonquian-speaking peoples along its banks. Its mouth lies at Point Lookout, Maryland.
tossups.r: It flows past Washington, D.C. For 10 points, name this river that forms much of the border between Maryland and Virginia.

tossups.p: In 1853, Ann Pamela Cunningham founded a ladies’ association that bought and preserved a famous plantation home on a hill overlooking this river in Virginia. That home’s owner had died there in 1799.
tossups.r: That home is Mount Vernon. For 10 points, name this river that flows past Washington, D.C., on its way to the Chesapeake Bay.

tossups.p: In 1846, Congress returned to Virginia the part of the federal district that lay on the southern side of this river, including the port of Alexandria and what is now Arlington.
tossups.r: The Residence Act of 1790 put the capital on this river. For 10 points, name this river between Washington, D.C., and Virginia.

tossups.p: The Arlington Memorial Bridge crosses this river to link the Lincoln Memorial with Arlington National Cemetery, and the Francis Scott Key Bridge crosses it at Georgetown. Farther south, the Woodrow Wilson Bridge carries Interstate 95 over it near Alexandria.
tossups.r: George Washington’s Mount Vernon also overlooks it. For 10 points, name this river that separates Washington, D.C., from Virginia.

tossups.p: The Monocacy [“muh-NOK-uh-see”] River and Antietam Creek, both sites of Civil War battles, flow into this river from Maryland, and the Shenandoah joins it at Harpers Ferry, West Virginia, after flowing north through a famous valley.
tossups.r: The Anacostia River joins it in Washington, D.C. For 10 points, name this river that empties into the Chesapeake Bay.

clues.t: Flows past Washington, D.C., the national capital built on its banks
Forms much of the border between Maryland and Virginia (and West Virginia)
George Washington’s home, Mount Vernon, overlooks it in Virginia
Empties into the Chesapeake Bay
Meets the Shenandoah River at Harpers Ferry, site of John Brown’s 1859 raid
Its Great Falls, just upstream from Washington, lie along the fall line; ships coming upriver could go no farther than Georgetown
The Chesapeake and Ohio Canal ran beside it from Georgetown to Cumberland, Maryland
The Residence Act of 1790 put the national capital on its banks
The Union’s main army in the East during the Civil War was named for it
Lee’s army crossed it to invade Maryland (1862) and retreated across it at Boteler’s Ford after the Battle of Antietam
Arlington National Cemetery lies across it from the Lincoln Memorial; the Arlington Memorial Bridge and the Francis Scott Key Bridge cross it
John Wilkes Booth crossed it by rowboat into Virginia while escaping (April 1865)
Maryland’s border runs along the low-water mark on its Virginia shore, so Maryland owns nearly all of the river there
John Quincy Adams broke ground for the canal on July 4, 1828; Justice William O. Douglas’s hike on its towpath later helped save it
George Washington was the first president of the Patowmack Company, which built canals around its rapids
Mount Vernon Conference (1785): Virginia and Maryland settled disputes over shipping and fishing on it, a step toward the Constitutional Convention
Thomas Jefferson said the view where it meets the Shenandoah was “worth a voyage across the Atlantic”
Its North Branch begins at the Fairfax Stone in West Virginia
Below Great Falls it rushes through Mather Gorge, named for the first director of the National Park Service
Washington, James Monroe, and Robert E. Lee were born in Westmoreland County, on the Northern Neck between it and the Rappahannock
John Quincy Adams liked to swim in it early in the morning; Theodore Roosevelt Island in it is a memorial
Captain John Smith explored it in 1608; it meets the Chesapeake at Point Lookout, Maryland
Ann Pamela Cunningham founded the Mount Vernon Ladies’ Association (1853), which bought and saved Washington’s home
In 1846, Congress gave the land south of it, including Alexandria, back to Virginia (retrocession)
Its tributaries include the Monocacy River, Antietam Creek, the Shenandoah, and the Anacostia

trap.title: River, bay, or tributary?
trap.body: The Potomac flows into the Chesapeake Bay, so bay clues and river clues get mixed up, and its tributaries, like the Shenandoah at Harpers Ferry and the Anacostia in Washington, D.C., are separate answers. The Rappahannock, farther south, runs past Ferry Farm, where George Washington spent much of his boyhood. A popular legend says Washington threw a silver dollar across the Potomac, though some versions place the throw at the Rappahannock, near that boyhood home.
trap.fix: Potomac clues: Washington, D.C., Mount Vernon, Great Falls, Harpers Ferry, the C&O Canal, and the Maryland–Virginia border. Shenandoah clues: its valley, Stonewall Jackson’s 1862 campaign, and flowing north into another river. Chesapeake Bay clues: an estuary, oysters and blue crabs, and the Chesapeake Bay Bridge.
trap.line: Real answer line: Potomac River (do not accept “Chesapeake Bay” or “Shenandoah River”)

topics.name: President pro tempore of the Senate
topics.kicker: Highest-ranking senator · Third in line for the presidency
topics.briefing: The Constitution makes the vice president the President of the Senate, but vice presidents are rarely there, so senators choose one of their own members to preside “for the time being,” which is what pro tempore means in Latin. By custom, the job goes to the longest-serving senator of the majority party, and it puts its holder third in line for the presidency. In 2023, Patty Murray of Washington became the first woman to hold it.
topics.answerHtml: President pro tempore of the Senate (or President pro tem; prompt on pro tempore or presiding officer; do not accept “President of the Senate,” “Vice President,” or “Speaker of the House”)
accept: president pro tempore of the senate
president pro tempore of the us senate
president pro tempore of the united states senate
president pro tem of the senate
reject: vice president of the united states
speaker of the house of representatives

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Article I, Section 3 of the Constitution says the Senate shall choose this officer “in the Absence of the Vice President, or when he shall exercise the Office of President of the United States.” Senators elect one of their own members to this post, and by custom they pick the longest-serving member of the majority party.
tossups.r: Its name includes a Latin phrase meaning “for the time being.” For 10 points, name this Senate office, third in the presidential line of succession.

tossups.p: Under the Presidential Succession Act of 1792, the holder of this office came next in line for the presidency after the vice president, even ahead of the Speaker of the House. An 1886 law dropped both of those congressional leaders from the line of succession, but a 1947 law brought them back.
tossups.r: That law placed this office right after the Speaker. For 10 points, name this Senate office, third in line for the presidency.

tossups.p: In 1868, Benjamin Wade of Ohio held this office, so he would have become president if the Senate had removed Andrew Johnson, who had no vice president. Some historians think a few senators voted to acquit Johnson partly because they did not want Wade, a Radical Republican, in the White House.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this office, whose holder presides over the Senate when the vice president is absent.

tossups.p: A popular legend says that David Rice Atchison of Missouri, who held this office, was president for one day in 1849, because Zachary Taylor would not take the oath of office on a Sunday. Historians reject that story, partly because Atchison never took the presidential oath himself.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this office, usually given to the longest-serving senator of the majority party.

tossups.p: In April 1789, the Senate chose John Langdon of New Hampshire as the first person to hold this office, so that he could count the electoral votes from the first presidential election before the vice president took office.
tossups.r: Its holder presides over the Senate whenever the vice president is away. For 10 points, name this office, third in line for the presidency.

tossups.p: Daniel Inouye [“in-NOH-ay”] of Hawaii, a World War II Medal of Honor recipient, became the first Asian American to hold this office in 2010. He took over from Robert Byrd of West Virginia, the longest-serving senator in history, who held this post until he died.
tossups.r: It usually goes to the majority party’s most senior senator. For 10 points, name this Senate office, third in line for the presidency.

tossups.p: Because the Chief Justice presides only when a sitting president is on trial, Patrick Leahy of Vermont presided over the 2021 Senate impeachment trial of Donald Trump, who had already left office, while holding this office. Leahy held this post twice, the second time until he retired in 2023.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this office, whose holder presides over the Senate when the vice president is absent.

tossups.p: In 2001, the Senate created an honorary “emeritus” version of this office for Strom Thurmond of South Carolina, who had held this office for much of the 1980s and 1990s. Thurmond kept serving in the Senate until he was 100 years old.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this office, usually held by the most senior senator of the majority party.

tossups.p: Arthur Vandenberg of Michigan held this office when he sponsored a 1948 resolution that paved the way for the NATO alliance. A former isolationist, Vandenberg also worked with President Harry Truman to win Senate support for the Marshall Plan.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this office, whose holder presides over the Senate when the vice president is absent.

tossups.p: In January 2025, Chuck Grassley of Iowa was elected to this office at the age of 91, returning to a post he had held from 2019 to 2021. He took over from Patty Murray of Washington, who in 2023 had become the first woman to hold it.
tossups.r: This office usually goes to the longest-serving senator of the majority party. For 10 points, name this office, third in line for the presidency.

tossups.p: Robert Byrd, who held this office several times, wrote a four-volume history of the Senate and often carried a copy of the Constitution in his pocket. Byrd, a West Virginian who became the longest-serving senator in history, last held this office from 2007 until his death in 2010.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this office, whose holder presides over the Senate when the vice president is away.

tossups.p: Holders of this office rarely preside over the Senate’s daily sessions in person; instead, junior senators of the majority party take turns holding the gavel. Unlike the vice president, the holder of this office may vote on any bill, not only to break ties.
tossups.r: This office’s name includes a Latin phrase meaning “for the time being.” For 10 points, name this office, third in line for the presidency.

tossups.p: In 1977, the Senate created a “deputy” version of this office for Hubert Humphrey, a former vice president who had failed to win the post of majority leader. Humphrey held that new post until his death in January 1978.
tossups.r: Under a 1947 law, the holder of the main office comes right after the Speaker in the line of succession. For 10 points, name this Senate office.

tossups.p: Thomas Ferry of Michigan held this office when he presided over the count of electoral votes in the disputed election of 1876, because Vice President Henry Wilson had died in office. In March 1877, Ferry announced that Rutherford B. Hayes had won by a single electoral vote.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this office, held by the senator who presides over the Senate when the vice president is absent.

tossups.p: Orrin Hatch of Utah held this office from 2015 to 2019, between Patrick Leahy and Chuck Grassley. Because the post goes to the most senior senator of whichever party holds a majority, it usually changes hands when control of the Senate flips.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this office, third in line for the presidency after the vice president and the Speaker of the House.

Presides over the Senate when the vice president, the official President of the Senate, is absent

trap.title: Which presiding officer?
trap.body: The Constitution makes the vice president the “President of the Senate,” so that answer is wrong here even though it sounds almost the same. The Senate majority leader, who runs the Senate’s day-to-day business, is a different job, and the Speaker of the House leads the House and comes just ahead of this office in the line of succession. Famous holders like Robert Byrd or Patty Murray can tempt you to buzz with a name when the question wants the office.
trap.fix: Listen for “for the time being,” “when the vice president is absent,” or “longest-serving senator of the majority party.” “Third in line” means the President pro tempore; “second in line” means the Speaker; “first in line” or “breaks ties” means the vice president.

topics.name: Republic of Texas
topics.kicker: Independent nation from 1836 to 1845 · Joined the U.S. as the 28th state
topics.briefing: For almost ten years, Texas was its own country, with its own president, army, navy, money, and flag. After winning independence from Mexico at San Jacinto in 1836, the Republic of Texas chose Sam Houston as its first elected president and later moved its capital from the young town of Houston to a new frontier city named Austin. In 1845, the United States annexed it as the 28th state, which helped start the Mexican-American War.
topics.answerHtml: Republic of Texas (or Texas Republic or Lone Star Republic; prompt on Texas)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In February 1846, this nation’s last president, Anson Jones, lowered its flag at a ceremony and declared that the nation was “no more.” Jones is sometimes called the “Architect of Annexation” for helping it join a much larger country.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this independent nation, led earlier by Sam Houston, that existed from 1836 until the United States annexed it.

tossups.p: In 1839, a commission picked a frontier village called Waterloo on the Colorado River as the site of a new capital, a spot favored by this nation’s second president, Mirabeau Lamar [“MEER-uh-boh luh-MAR”]. Lamar also pushed to set aside public land to pay for schools and universities.
tossups.r: The new capital was named for Stephen F. Austin. For 10 points, name this nation that existed from 1836 to 1845.

tossups.p: In December 1842, Angelina Eberly fired a cannon to stop men sent by this nation’s president from hauling government records out of Austin, in the so-called Archive War. That president had argued that Austin was too exposed to attack.
tossups.r: That president was Sam Houston. For 10 points, name this nation that existed from 1836 to 1845, before it joined the United States.

tossups.p: Interim president David Burnet signed the Treaties of Velasco [“veh-LAHS-koh”] on behalf of this nation, in which a captured general promised to pull his army back beyond the Rio Grande. That general’s government rejected the treaties and refused to recognize this nation’s independence.
tossups.r: That general, Santa Anna, had been captured after the Battle of San Jacinto. For 10 points, name this nation, led by Sam Houston, that existed from 1836 to 1845.

tossups.p: This nation claimed the Rio Grande as its southern and western border, but Mexico insisted that the boundary was the Nueces [“noo-AY-sis”] River, farther north. After the United States took over this nation’s claim, a clash in the land between those rivers helped start a war in 1846.
tossups.r: John Tyler signed the resolution to annex it just before leaving office. For 10 points, name this nation, once led by Sam Houston.

tossups.p: In the Compromise of 1850, the state formed from this former nation gave up its claims to land in present-day New Mexico in exchange for 10 million dollars to help pay off this nation’s old debts. This nation had printed paper money called “redbacks” that quickly lost most of its value.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this nation, led by presidents such as Sam Houston and Mirabeau Lamar, that existed from 1836 to 1845.

tossups.p: France became the first European country to recognize this nation, in 1839, and its diplomat Alphonse Dubois de Saligny [“sah-leen-YEE”] later had a legation built in this nation’s capital. Andrew Jackson had recognized this nation on his last full day as president, in March 1837.
tossups.r: Its capitals included Houston and Austin. For 10 points, name this nation, whose first elected president was Sam Houston.

tossups.p: In 1839, this nation replaced a flag showing one large gold star on a blue field, often named for David Burnet, with a new design. The new flag had a blue vertical stripe holding a single white star, next to horizontal white and red stripes.
tossups.r: That “Lone Star” flag later became a state flag. For 10 points, name this nation that joined the United States in 1845.

tossups.p: In this nation’s first national election, in September 1836, voters overwhelmingly approved seeking annexation, and Stephen F. Austin finished far behind in the race for president. The winner of that race was barred from serving two terms in a row, so Mirabeau Lamar succeeded him.
tossups.r: That winner, Sam Houston, later served a second term. For 10 points, name this nation that the United States annexed in 1845.

tossups.p: In 1841, an expedition of about 300 soldiers and merchants from this nation tried to take over the Santa Fe trade, but New Mexican forces captured them and sent them on a long march to Mexico City. This nation’s president, Mirabeau Lamar, had sent that expedition.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this nation, whose first elected president, Sam Houston, had won independence at San Jacinto.

tossups.p: Lorenzo de Zavala [“dee zuh-VAH-luh”], a politician born in Yucatán, Mexico, served as this nation’s first vice president on an interim basis in 1836. He had signed this nation’s declaration of independence at Washington-on-the-Brazos in March of that year.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this nation, whose flag had a single white star, that existed from 1836 to 1845.

tossups.p: This nation’s second president reversed his predecessor’s more peaceful policy toward Native nations, and in 1839 his army drove most of the Cherokee people out of its territory. That president had earlier served as vice president under his predecessor.
tossups.r: That president, Mirabeau Lamar, served between Sam Houston’s two terms. For 10 points, name this nation that existed from 1836 to 1845.

tossups.p: After the U.S. Senate rejected a treaty to annex this nation in 1844, Congress used a joint resolution, which needed only a simple majority in each house, to do the job instead. John Tyler signed that resolution just days before he left office in March 1845.
tossups.r: Later that year, its voters approved joining the Union. For 10 points, name this nation that became the 28th state in December 1845.

tossups.p: Brothers Augustus and John Allen founded a town on Buffalo Bayou in 1836 and named it for a general, hoping it would become this nation’s capital. Their plan worked, and that town served as this nation’s capital from 1837 to 1839.
tossups.r: That town was named for Sam Houston, this nation’s first elected president. For 10 points, name this nation that existed from 1836 to 1845.

tossups.p: This nation’s 1836 constitution protected slavery, so many Northerners opposed adding it to the United States, and Martin Van Buren turned down its request to join in 1837. James K. Polk won the presidency in 1844 partly by promising to bring this nation into the Union.
tossups.r: It became the 28th state in 1845. For 10 points, name this nation, led by Sam Houston, that broke away from Mexico in 1836.

trap.title: Nation, war, or state?
trap.body: The Texas Revolution (1835–1836) was the war that created this nation, and the Alamo and San Jacinto were battles in it, so naming the war or a battle is wrong when the question asks for “this nation” or “this republic.” Other short-lived republics have their own answer lines, such as the Bear Flag Republic (California, 1846) and the Republic of West Florida (1810), which also flew a flag with a single white star. Saying just “Texas” earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this nation,” “this republic,” or “this country” with Sam Houston, Mirabeau Lamar, Anson Jones, the Archive War, or annexation wants the Republic of Texas. If you are prompted, add “Republic of.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Republic of Texas (or Texas Republic or Lone Star Republic; prompt on Texas)

topics.name: Savannah, Georgia
topics.kicker: Georgia’s oldest city, founded 1733 · End of Sherman’s March to the Sea
topics.briefing: In 1733, James Oglethorpe and a shipload of English colonists climbed a bluff above a river near the Atlantic and laid out Savannah, the first city in Georgia, around a grid of shady public squares, most of which still exist. Eli Whitney built his cotton gin at a plantation nearby, and in 1864 General William T. Sherman ended his March to the Sea here, offering the city to Abraham Lincoln as a “Christmas gift.” Juliette Gordon Low founded the Girl Scouts here in 1912.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: With help from the interpreter Mary Musgrove, this city’s founder made friends with Tomochichi [“TOH-moh-CHEE-chee”], the leader of the Yamacraw [“YAM-uh-kraw”] people, who allowed English colonists to settle on a bluff above a river. Tomochichi later sailed to London and met King George II.
tossups.r: That founder was James Oglethorpe. For 10 points, name this city founded in 1733, the first city in the colony of Georgia.

tossups.p: The bench scenes in the film _Forrest Gump_ were shot in this city’s Chippewa Square, one of 22 surviving public squares out of the 24 laid out as the city grew. Those squares follow the founder’s plan, in which each neighborhood, or ward, was built around a central square.
tossups.r: That plan was drawn up by James Oglethorpe. For 10 points, name this city on the Georgia coast, the colony’s first settlement.

tossups.p: In October 1779, the Polish cavalry officer Casimir Pulaski [“puh-LASS-kee”] was mortally wounded in a failed French and American attack on this British-held city. Volunteers from the French colony of Saint-Domingue [“san doh-MANG”], now Haiti, also fought in that siege.
tossups.r: The British held this city for most of the rest of the war. For 10 points, name this Georgia port founded by James Oglethorpe in 1733.

tossups.p: At Mulberry Grove, a plantation upriver from this city owned by Catharine Greene, the widow of General Nathanael Greene, a young Yale graduate built a machine in 1793 that pulled the seeds out of cotton. The plantation’s manager, Phineas Miller, became that inventor’s business partner.
tossups.r: That inventor was Eli Whitney. For 10 points, name this Georgia port city founded by James Oglethorpe.

tossups.p: In December 1864, Union soldiers stormed Fort McAllister, opening a supply line to the sea south of this city. Days later, Confederate general William Hardee pulled his troops out across the river into South Carolina, and Union troops marched in.
tossups.r: Their commander then offered this city to Abraham Lincoln as a “Christmas gift.” For 10 points, name this Georgia city where William T. Sherman ended his March to the Sea.

tossups.p: In January 1865, Secretary of War Edwin Stanton and a Union general met with a group of Black church leaders in this city, led by the Baptist minister Garrison Frazier. Days later, that general issued Special Field Orders No. 15 here, setting aside coastal land for freed families.
tossups.r: That general, William T. Sherman, had just ended his March to the Sea here. For 10 points, name this Georgia port.

tossups.p: In 1819, a ship named for this city left its port on May 22 and became the first steamship to cross the Atlantic Ocean, though it used its sails for most of the trip. That departure date is now celebrated as National Maritime Day.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Georgia port city, where Juliette Gordon Low founded the Girl Scouts in 1912.

tossups.p: In April 1862, Union rifled cannons fired from Tybee Island broke through the thick brick walls of Fort Pulaski, which guarded the river approach to this city. That success showed that old masonry forts could no longer stand up to modern artillery.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Georgia port, which William T. Sherman captured at the end of his March to the Sea.

tossups.p: In March 1861, Confederate Vice President Alexander Stephens gave his “Cornerstone Speech” in this city, saying that the new Confederacy rested on slavery. Before the Civil War, this city’s port shipped huge amounts of cotton grown across Georgia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this city that William T. Sherman offered to Abraham Lincoln as a “Christmas gift” in 1864.

tossups.p: John Wesley, the founder of Methodism, served as a minister in this city in the 1730s, and George Whitefield [“WIT-feeld”] founded the Bethesda orphanage nearby in 1740. Jewish settlers arrived in this city only months after it was founded.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this city founded by James Oglethorpe, the first in the colony of Georgia.

tossups.p: The songwriter Johnny Mercer, who wrote the words to “Moon River,” and the author Flannery O’Connor were both born in this city. John Berendt’s 1994 nonfiction bestseller _Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil_ is set here.
tossups.r: Juliette Gordon Low founded the Girl Scouts here in 1912. For 10 points, name this Georgia city founded by James Oglethorpe.

tossups.p: In 1912, a woman inspired by Robert Baden-Powell gathered 18 girls in this city to form the first troop of a group first called the American Girl Guides, which took a new name the next year.
tossups.r: That woman, Juliette Gordon Low, founded the Girl Scouts. For 10 points, name this Georgia city, where James Oglethorpe’s colonists landed in 1733.

tossups.p: Every March, the fountain in this city’s Forsyth Park is dyed green before one of the largest St. Patrick’s Day parades in the United States. An art and design college founded here in 1978, known as SCAD, has restored many of this city’s historic buildings.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Georgia port city, where Sherman’s March to the Sea ended in 1864.

tossups.p: A ship named for this city, launched in 1959, became the world’s first nuclear-powered cargo and passenger ship. This city’s port, on the river that forms much of the border between Georgia and South Carolina, is one of the busiest container ports in the United States.
tossups.r: James Oglethorpe founded it in 1733. For 10 points, name this city, the oldest in Georgia.

tossups.p: The colony that began in this city was meant partly as a buffer between South Carolina and Spanish Florida, and its Trustees at first banned slavery there. This city’s founder had led a campaign in Parliament to improve conditions in debtors’ prisons.
tossups.r: That founder, James Oglethorpe, landed here in 1733. For 10 points, name this first city of the colony of Georgia.
